title: FBI Will No Longer Investigate ICE Confrontations, Agents Told
excerpt: A new directive tells federal agents the FBI will stop probing violent encounters between ICE officers and civilians, removing the primary oversight mechanism as fatal shootings mount.
body:
• Federal agents have been told the FBI will no longer investigate confrontations between ICE officers and civilians, according to The New York Times.
  • The directive comes amid at least 10 agency-involved firearm discharges in 2026, including multiple fatal shootings during traffic stops.
  • Nearly 200 members of Congress, led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, have demanded independent investigations into recent ICE-related deaths.
  • The move effectively removes the primary federal mechanism for holding immigration enforcement officers accountable for use of force.

The Directive

Federal agents have been informed that the FBI will no longer investigate confrontations involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, according to a report by The New York Times. The directive strips away what had been the principal federal mechanism for reviewing use-of-force incidents by immigration agents, at a time when such encounters have turned increasingly violent.

The FBI has traditionally served as the lead agency investigating federal law enforcement shootings and use-of-force incidents, providing a layer of independent oversight. Without that function, accountability for ICE operations during arrests, traffic stops, and other enforcement actions falls into a gap that local law enforcement has shown little willingness to fill.

Mounting Death Toll

The policy shift comes against a backdrop of escalating violence. There have been at least 10 ICE-involved firearm discharges in 2026. Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed during a traffic stop on July 7 when, according to ICE, he attempted to evade arrest and rammed an agent's vehicle. In Minnesota, 37-year-old Renee Good was fatally shot during another traffic stop. Two deaths in Maine and Texas have also drawn scrutiny.

"Two fathers were shot and killed by ICE agents in unmarked cars hiding behind masks, and these individuals were not even targets of any investigation."

— Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-WA)

Rep. Jayapal, the Indian-American congresswoman from Washington state, sent a formal letter backed by nearly 200 members of Congress demanding immediate, independent investigations from the Department of Homeland Security.

Traffic Stops Under Fire

The controversy centers largely on ICE's growing use of vehicle stops for immigration enforcement. Former officials and policing experts have questioned whether agents receive adequate training for roadside encounters — historically among the most dangerous situations in law enforcement. Unlike local police who conduct traffic stops routinely, ICE agents historically relied on other enforcement methods.

DHS briefly paused most vehicle stops after the fatal incidents, but President Trump ordered them reinstated within hours. "We CANNOT give up one of I.C.E.'s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Impact on Immigrant Communities

For the roughly 4.5 million Indian-Americans and millions of other immigrants in the United States, the removal of FBI oversight compounds existing fears about enforcement operations. Community advocacy groups say the directive sends a signal that agents can operate without meaningful accountability.

The directive also raises questions about ongoing investigations. ProPublica has documented cases where local police deferred entirely to the FBI at shooting scenes — a pattern that leaves no investigative body if the FBI steps aside.

What's Next

Congressional Democrats have called for the Justice Department's inspector general to step in as an alternative oversight mechanism. Whether that office has the capacity or mandate to investigate individual use-of-force incidents remains unclear. Civil liberties organizations are expected to challenge the directive in court, arguing it violates due process protections.
